subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
past_paper_reference: CUET UG Mass Media Past Papers (2022-2024)

questions.question: When a political leader or motivational speaker delivers a formal address to a large physical gathering seated in an auditorium, which level of communication is occurring?
options: A) Public communication
B) Intrapersonal communication
C) Dyadic communication
D) Subliminal communication
questions.explanation: Public communication involves a single speaker addressing a large audience face-to-face in a structured, formal public setting.

questions.question: In the study of non-verbal communication, the discipline of 'Oculesics' specifically investigates:
options: A) The physical distance maintained between conversational partners
B) The role of eye contact, gaze behavior, pupil dilation, and blinking in interpersonal interaction
C) The volume and musical pitch of human vocal speech
D) The cultural etiquette of greeting handshakes and bows
questions.explanation: Oculesics is the study of eye behavior—eye contact, eye movement, gaze avoidance, and pupil dilation—as non-verbal signals of interest, trust, or dominance.

questions.question: In Theodore Newcomb's ABX co-orientation model of communication, what do the letters A, B, and X represent?
options: A) Author, Book, and Xerox machine
B) Actor, Broadcast, and X-ray radiation
C) Two communicators (A and B) and an external topic, issue, or object of common orientation (X)
D) Audience, Broadcaster, and Transmitter
questions.explanation: Newcomb's ABX model focuses on balance and symmetry between two communicating parties (A and B) regarding their mutual orientation toward a common topic or object (X).

questions.question: The foundational 1972 Chapel Hill election study by Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw demonstrated which famous media effect?
options: A) The media forces every voter to cast their ballot for the wealthiest candidate
B) Television broadcasts make all viewers completely forget the names of political candidates
C) Reading newspapers causes people to become completely apathetic toward all public elections
D) The media may not tell people what to think, but they are stunningly successful in telling people what to think ABOUT
questions.explanation: McCombs and Shaw proved Agenda-Setting theory: by giving high salience to select issues in news coverage, the press influences which issues the public considers most important.

questions.question: In Stuart Hall's Encoding/Decoding model, when an audience member accepts the dominant media narrative in broad terms but modifies it to fit their own personal local experience, they take:
options: A) A Negotiated code reading position
B) A Dominant-Hegemonic reading position
C) An Oppositional reading position
D) A Completely Passive hypodermic position
questions.explanation: Hall identified 3 decoding positions: Dominant-Hegemonic (fully accepts preferred meaning), Negotiated (accepts broad ideology but modifies for local contradictions), and Oppositional (rejects preferred meaning).

questions.question: In George Gerbner's Cultivation Analysis, the concept of 'Resonance' occurs when:
options: A) Two radio transmitters operate on the exact same electromagnetic megahertz frequency
B) Television viewers see real-world events in their daily lives that mirror the violent portrayals on screen, producing a double dose of cultivation and amplified fear
C) Television actors sing in harmony with the studio sound recording orchestra
D) A viewer smashes their television screen during an intense dramatic scene
questions.explanation: Resonance occurs when an audience's lived reality aligns with the televised depiction; this congruence reinforces and intensifies the cultivated television worldview.

questions.sub_topic: Charles Sanders Peirce: Icon, Index, and Symbol
questions.question: In Charles Sanders Peirce's semiotic classification, why is 'Smoke' an 'Index' of fire, whereas the word 'FIRE' is a 'Symbol'?
options: A) Smoke looks physically identical to the shape of fire, while the word fire is an optical illusion
B) Smoke can only be seen during nighttime hours, while words can only be read in daylight
C) Smoke has a physical, existential causal connection to fire, whereas the word 'FIRE' is an arbitrary, learned cultural convention
D) Smoke is a chemical substance produced by wood, while words are produced by television cables
questions.explanation: Peirce's triad: Icons resemble their object (portrait); Indices have a direct physical/causal link (smoke -> fire, footprint); Symbols rely on arbitrary social agreement (words).

questions.question: In professional journalism, the grave ethical offense of taking someone else's written words, investigative work, or ideas and publishing them as one's own without attribution is called:
options: A) Syndication
B) Embargo
C) Dateline
D) Plagiarism
questions.explanation: Plagiarism is the unethical misappropriation and unauthorized presentation of another writer's intellectual expression as one's own, destroying journalistic credibility.

questions.question: In a newspaper, a brief directional note at the bottom of a front-page article (such as 'Continued on Page 4') that guides the reader to the continuation of the story is called a:
options: A) Jump line
B) Kicker
C) Slug
D) Banner
questions.explanation: A jump line directs the reader to the specific interior page where a story originating on the front page is continued.

questions.question: An official, formal government policy statement issued directly to news media organizations (such as following a bilateral international summit) is termed a:
options: A) Classified Memo
B) Press Communiqué
C) Radio Jingle
D) Anonymous Leak
questions.explanation: A press communiqué is an official formal announcement issued by a government or authoritative body summarizing conclusions or policies.

questions.question: In the law of defamation, what is the crucial legal distinction between 'Libel' and 'Slander'?
options: A) Libel applies only to foreign citizens, while slander applies only to local residents
B) Libel is punishable only by community service, while slander carries mandatory capital punishment
C) Libel is defamatory communication published in a permanent, recorded form (such as print, broadcast, or online text), while Slander is spoken, transitory verbal defamation
D) Libel can only be committed by television networks, while slander is committed exclusively in books
questions.explanation: Libel is written, printed, or broadcast defamation in permanent form; Slander is oral, spoken, or temporary unrecorded defamatory communication.

questions.question: In a major national newspaper or news agency, what is the role of a 'Bureau Chief' stationed in a major regional capital or foreign city?
options: A) To physically operate the printing press machines in the regional factory warehouse
B) To deliver freshly printed newspapers door-to-door on early morning delivery routes
C) To audit the corporate tax returns of commercial automobile manufacturing companies
D) To lead, manage, and assign coverage to the team of correspondents operating in that specific city or region, coordinating reporting with head office
questions.explanation: A Bureau Chief heads a regional or foreign bureau, directing correspondents, managing local news flow, and ensuring high-quality coverage from that territory.

questions.question: Why is the preservation of source confidentiality considered the most sacred, non-negotiable canon of investigative reporting?
options: A) Because revealing sources' identities exposes whistleblowers to physical danger, job loss, or legal retaliation, drying up future insider disclosures vital for public scrutiny
B) Because reporters are paid a financial bonus whenever they keep secrets from their editors
C) Because police departments require journalists to submit all informant names in sealed envelopes
D) Because source confidentiality is legally required only when reporting on collegiate sporting events
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects whistleblowers from retribution, ensuring that courageous insiders continue to expose corruption and systemic wrongdoing to journalists in the public interest.

questions.sub_topic: Press Council of India Act, 1978: Powers and Limitations
questions.question: Why is the statutory Press Council of India (PCI) often described as a 'Paper Tiger' by legal commentators and media critics?
options: A) Because its council members are required by law to wear paper masks during formal hearings

B) Because while it can summon witnesses, hold inquiries, and warn, admonish, or censure an errant newspaper or journalist, it possesses no punitive statutory power to impose fines or suspend licenses
C) Because it only regulates publications printed on handmade recycled rice paper sheets
D) Because it was permanently shut down and replaced by the Ministry of Telecommunications in 1999
questions.explanation: The PCI is a quasi-judicial watchdog enforcing moral and ethical standards; it can admonish or censure newspapers, but cannot levy fines, award damages, or revoke publishing licenses.

questions.question: When a branded commercial item (such as an Apple laptop or a Coca-Cola can) is prominently displayed and used by characters inside a feature film or television drama, this practice is known as:
options: A) Classified Advertising
B) Direct Mail Solicitation
C) Product Placement (or Embedded Marketing)
D) Print Brochure Distribution
questions.explanation: Product placement integrates branded goods or services seamlessly into non-advertising media (movies, TV shows, video games) for subliminal exposure.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.question: During a corporate crisis (such as an industrial chemical leak or major data breach), what is the most critical public relations best practice regarding media communication?
options: A) Allow all employees to give conflicting personal opinions to television reporters
B) Disconnect all telephone lines and refuse to answer any questions from the press indefinitely
C) Blame innocent consumers publicly on social media to protect corporate stock prices
D) Appoint a single, well-trained official spokesperson who communicates accurate, transparent, and consistent information promptly
questions.explanation: Crisis PR mandates speaking with one unified, authoritative, compassionate, and transparent voice through a designated spokesperson to prevent rumors and panic.

questions.sub_topic: Copywriting: The Anatomy of Print Ad Structure
questions.question: In print advertising composition, which structural element sits directly beneath the main headline to expand on the creative hook and transition the reader smoothly into the body copy?
options: A) Sub-headline (or Subhead)
B) Mandatory Legal Disclaimer
C) Trademark Registration Seal
D) Corporate Fax Number
questions.explanation: A subhead (sub-headline) bridges the headline and body copy, elaborating on the core promise and maintaining reader momentum.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Media
questions.sub_topic: Cost Per Thousand (CPM) in Media Planning
questions.question: In advertising media planning, what does the fundamental measurement metric 'CPM' (Cost Per Mille) calculate?
options: A) The cost of printing one thousand physical paper copies of a corporate brochure
B) The cost an advertiser pays to deliver one thousand commercial impressions or exposures to the target audience
C) The monetary fee paid to a celebrity actor for speaking one thousand words on television
D) The number of miles a billboard delivery truck drives across the country per year
questions.explanation: CPM (Cost Per Mille, Latin for thousand) evaluates media efficiency by calculating the cost to reach 1,000 readers, viewers, or web visitors across different media vehicles.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.question: In corporate public relations and government relations, 'Lobbying' is defined as the practice of:
options: A) Bribing judicial magistrates with cash bags inside courthouse lobby corridors
B) Constructing hotel lobbies for foreign tourist delegations visiting national monuments
C) Informing, educating, and attempting to ethically persuade lawmakers and government officials to enact or amend policies beneficial to an industry or cause
D) Hacking into government servers to erase corporate tax filing databases
questions.explanation: Lobbying involves advocating for specific policy outcomes by presenting research, industry data, and stakeholder viewpoints to legislators and regulatory officials.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Regulations
questions.sub_topic: Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
questions.question: Under the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 in India, commercial advertisements are strictly prohibited from claiming:
options: A) That prescription medicines can be purchased at licensed retail chemist shops
B) That pharmaceutical companies conduct clinical trials on laboratory animals
C) That certified doctors possess medical degrees from recognized universities
D) Miraculous cures, magical remedies, or treatments for certain specified diseases and conditions (such as cancer, diabetes, blindness, and sexual disorders)
questions.explanation: The 1954 Act criminalizes misleading ads promoting magic remedies, talismans, or miraculous cures for grave medical conditions like diabetes, cancer, or epilepsy.

questions.question: Which standard television camera shot frames a human subject comfortably from roughly the waist up, capturing both facial expressions and upper-body gestures during interviews?
options: A) Medium Shot (MS)
B) Extreme Wide Shot (EWS)
C) Extreme Close-Up (ECU)
D) Aerial Satellite Shot
questions.explanation: A Medium Shot (MS) frames an actor from the waist or hips up, balancing facial emotion with hand gestures and surrounding context.

questions.question: In a television studio control room, what is the electronic control console used by the technical director to select and switch between multiple live camera feeds called?
options: A) Sound Equalizer
B) Video Switcher (or Production Switcher)
C) Audio Compressor
D) Acoustic Diffuser
questions.explanation: The video switcher (or vision mixer) is the central console in the control room used to switch, cut, dissolve, and composite live video feeds.

questions.question: In standard three-point television lighting, what is the specific operational function of the 'Fill Light'?
options: A) To flood the studio floor with blinding overhead light so cameras can autofocus
B) To illuminate the camera operator's shoes so they do not trip over audio cables
C) To soften and fill in the harsh, deep shadows created on the subject's face by the primary key light without creating new competing shadows
D) To project colorful psychedelic patterns onto the rear cyclorama backdrop
questions.explanation: The Fill Light sits opposite the Key Light, filling in the shadows cast by the Key to control scene contrast and soften shadow harshness.

questions.sub_topic: Rule of Thirds in Screen Composition
questions.question: In television camerawork and photography, what is the guideline of the 'Rule of Thirds'?
options: A) Ensure that every television program features exactly three actors in every scene
B) Charge viewers three times the monthly subscription fee for watching news broadcasts
C) Divide the studio floor into three equal triangular zones where cameras cannot enter
D) Divide the frame into a 3x3 grid with two horizontal and two vertical lines, placing important visual subjects along the lines or at their intersection points
questions.explanation: The Rule of Thirds places visual points of interest along imaginary grid lines or their four intersection power points, creating dynamic, balanced visual compositions.

questions.sub_topic: Match on Action in Continuity Editing
questions.question: In television and film continuity editing, what occurs during a 'Match on Action' cut?
options: A) An editor cuts from one camera shot to another at the precise moment an actor performs an action (e.g., opening a door), seamlessly continuing the motion across shots
B) The editor cuts between two completely unrelated action scenes occurring in different centuries
C) The camera operator drops the camera while running after a moving sports car
D) The audio soundtrack is played backwards while the screen turns completely blank
questions.explanation: Matching on action splices two different angles of the same physical movement at the moment of motion, masking the cut and maintaining continuous action illusion.

questions.sub_topic: Television Systems: PAL vs NTSC Broadcast Standards
questions.question: Historically, which analog television broadcasting standard—operating at 625 horizontal lines of resolution and 25 frames per second (50 Hz)—was adopted by Doordarshan in India?
options: A) NTSC (National Television System Committee)
B) PAL (Phase Alternating Line)
C) SECAM (Séquentiel Couleur à Mémoire)
D) ATSC (Advanced Television Systems Committee)
questions.explanation: India and most European/Commonwealth nations adopted the PAL system (625 lines / 25 fps / 50 Hz power grid), whereas the US and Japan used NTSC (525 lines / 29.97 fps / 60 Hz).

questions.question: Why must radio presenters and studio guests always wear closed-back 'Headphones' while speaking into open studio microphones during a live broadcast?
options: A) To physically keep their ears warm during cold winter broadcast mornings
B) To listen to private telephone conversations conducted by studio executives
C) To monitor their own vocal level and studio sound while preventing audio feedback loop squeals into the open microphones
D) To prevent dangerous electromagnetic radio waves from entering their brain
questions.explanation: Studio monitors must be muted when mics are live to prevent ear-piercing acoustic feedback; presenters wear closed-back cans to hear program audio without mic bleed.

questions.sub_topic: Audio Fade: Fade In vs Fade Out
questions.question: In radio audio editing and mixing, what does a 'Fade In' describe?
options: A) A sudden abrupt cut that instantly silences all broadcast audio channels
B) A gradual decrease in audio volume until it reaches complete silence
C) A technical malfunction that causes speech to play at triple speed
D) A gradual, smooth increase in the volume level of a sound track or voice from total silence to full audible volume
questions.explanation: A fade-in gradually increases volume from silence to audible level; a fade-out smoothly decreases audio into silence.

questions.question: In a radio news bulletin, a short recorded excerpt of an eyewitness or public official speaking in their own voice is called a:
options: A) Sound Bite (or Actuality)
B) Jingle
C) Foley
D) Cue card
questions.explanation: A sound bite (in radio, called an 'actuality' or 'grab') is a short audio clip capturing the spoken voice of an interviewee or newsmaker.

questions.question: In radio music programming and audio editing, what happens during a 'Cross-Fade' between two audio tracks?
options: A) Both audio tracks are permanently deleted from the computer editing software
B) The first audio track gradually fades out while the second audio track simultaneously fades in over it, creating a seamless musical transition without silence
C) The audio mixer reverses the polarity of the speakers, causing physical smoke to emerge
D) The presenter stops talking and leaves the radio studio for forty-five minutes
questions.explanation: A cross-fade smoothly blends two overlapping audio clips: Track A fades down as Track B fades up, avoiding jarring dead air or harsh abrupt cuts.

questions.question: In terrestrial commercial radio broadcasting, why is unintended 'Dead Air' (unplanned silence on air) considered a severe emergency?
options: A) Dead air causes the physical broadcast transmitter tower to collapse onto the ground
B) Silence on radio causes lightning strikes to hit the broadcast studio building
C) Listeners assume the station has lost its transmission signal or shut down, prompting them to instantly retune their radio dials to competing stations
D) Station owners are legally sent to federal prison if silence lasts for two seconds
questions.explanation: Dead air (unintended silence) breaks the auditory connection; listeners assume equipment failure and switch stations, losing advertising ratings.

questions.sub_topic: SITE Experiment: Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (1975-76)
questions.question: In Indian broadcasting and developmental communication history, why is the 1975–1976 'SITE' (Satellite Instructional Television Experiment) regarded as a world milestone?
options: A) It launched the first commercial cable music television network in Southeast Asia
B) It allowed rural villagers to purchase international stock shares using satellite pagers
C) It replaced all human school teachers in India with automated robotic computers
D) It used NASA's ATS-6 satellite to beam educational television programming directly to community television sets across 2,400 remote Indian villages for agriculture, health, and primary education
questions.explanation: Led by Vikram Sarabhai and ISRO, SITE was the world's largest social communication experiment, broadcasting community education directly to rural India via satellite.

questions.question: In the motion picture filmmaking process, who is the creative artist responsible for conceiving the narrative story, developing characters, and writing the dialogue and screenplay?
options: A) Screenwriter (or Scriptwriter)
B) Gaffer
C) Key Grip
D) Colorist
questions.explanation: The screenwriter writes the blueprint of the film—the screenplay—detailing character arcs, scene descriptions, actions, and spoken dialogue.

questions.sub_topic: First Indian Talkie Film Star: Master Vithal and Zubeida
questions.question: Who was the celebrated female lead actress who starred opposite Master Vithal in India's first sound-and-talkie film 'Alam Ara' (1931)?
options: A) Devika Rani
B) Zubeida
C) Nargis
D) Madhubala
questions.explanation: Zubeida played the female lead in Ardeshir Irani's historic talkie 'Alam Ara' (1931), making her one of the earliest talkie stars in Indian cinema history.

questions.sub_topic: Jump Cut Definition and Psychological Impact
questions.question: In cinematic editing, a 'Jump Cut' is created when two sequential shots of the same subject are taken from camera positions that vary only slightly, causing:
options: A) The physical camera to jump into the air and land on the director's head
B) The film projection screen to turn completely purple for twenty minutes
C) A jarring, visible skip in action or time that shatters spatial-temporal continuity and calls attention to the editing process
D) A seamless, invisible match on action that no viewer can possibly notice
questions.explanation: A jump cut violates continuity rules by jumping forward in time between nearly identical camera setups, creating a visible stutter or jarring skip.

questions.question: Which of the following was a hallmark aesthetic characteristic of the French New Wave film movement in the late 1950s and 1960s (led by Godard, Truffaut, and Rohmer)?
options: A) Rigid adherence to elaborate classical Hollywood studio backlot sets and glamour lighting
B) Complete ban on all outdoor daylight filming in the streets of Paris
C) Exclusively using computer-generated 3D graphics and futuristic animated robots
D) Handheld camera work, natural location shooting, improvisation, direct sound recording, and self-reflexive jump cuts
questions.explanation: The French New Wave broke conventional studio filmmaking with portable lightweight cameras, authentic location shoots, improvisation, and dynamic jump cutting.

questions.topic: Cinema: Film Festivals and Parallel Cinema
questions.question: Established in 1975 (amalgamating the Film Finance Corporation and Indian Motion Pictures Export Corporation), the primary mandate of the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) in India is to:
options: A) Finance, produce, and promote high-quality, socially meaningful Indian parallel and independent cinema, fostering regional artistic talent
B) Censor and ban all foreign motion pictures from being screened in Indian cinema theaters
C) Produce commercial high-budget action films starring international Hollywood actors
D) Collect municipal sales taxes on popcorn and soft drink concession stands in movie multiplexes
questions.explanation: NFDC played a central role in nurturing Indian Parallel Cinema, funding seminal films by Ray, Sen, Benegal, Nihalani, Ketan Mehta, and Mira Nair.

questions.sub_topic: Sergei Eisenstein's Five Methods of Montage
questions.question: In early film theory, Soviet director Sergei Eisenstein articulated five distinct methods of montage: Metric, Rhythmic, Tonal, Overtonal, and:
options: A) Commercial Montage
B) Intellectual Montage
C) Mechanical Montage
D) Linear Montage
questions.explanation: Eisenstein's five methods of montage are: Metric (tempo/shot length), Rhythmic (action match), Tonal (emotional mood), Overtonal (synthesis of tones), and Intellectual (collision of ideas).

questions.question: In digital social media culture, a humorous image, video, or piece of text that is rapidly copied, altered with clever captions, and spread virally across internet platforms is a:
options: A) Firewall
B) Modem
C) Meme
D) Router
questions.explanation: An internet meme (derived from Richard Dawkins' concept) is a cultural unit or joke that replicates and mutates rapidly across digital networks.

questions.question: In online social interactions, the deceptive practice of creating a fake personal profile with stolen photographs to trick someone into a fraudulent romantic or financial relationship is known as:
options: A) Phishing
B) Trolling
C) Blogging
D) Catfishing
questions.explanation: Catfishing refers to adopting a fictional online identity (often using someone else's photos) to deceive, manipulate, or defraud victims on social/dating platforms.

questions.sub_topic: Social Media in Mobilizing Social Movements
questions.question: How did social media platforms (like Twitter and Facebook) function during mass democratic uprisings (such as the 2011 Arab Spring and the Nirbhaya protests in India)?
options: A) As rapid, decentralized tools for coordinating protests, bypassing state media censorship, sharing eyewitness documentation, and rallying global solidarity
B) As state-controlled surveillance weapons that permanently prevented citizens from meeting in person
C) As platforms that charged protesters fifty dollars for every text message sent during rallies
D) As obsolete technologies that had zero influence on the dissemination of protest news
questions.explanation: Social networks enabled decentralized coordination, real-time documentation of abuses, and sidestepping state-controlled broadcast gatekeepers to mobilize citizens.

questions.question: How does an online 'Echo Chamber' exacerbate political and social polarization in contemporary society?
options: A) It physically forces users to yell loudly into their smartphone microphones during debates
B) Users interact predominantly with like-minded individuals, continuously reinforcing shared biases while insulating themselves from opposing viewpoints and critical evidence
C) It causes computer speakers to repeat every spoken sentence twenty-five times
D) It shuts down all social media accounts belonging to political party candidates
questions.explanation: Echo chambers entrench dogmatism: self-selected like-minded networks confirm and amplify each other's beliefs while discrediting or ignoring dissenting evidence.

questions.question: Investigative studies into social video platforms (such as YouTube recommendations) revealed that optimizing algorithms purely for 'Watch Time' and 'Retention' often led to:
options: A) The automatic shutdown of computer monitors after twenty minutes of educational viewing
B) The permanent deletion of all videos discussing historical science or natural mathematics
C) The 'Rabbit Hole' phenomenon, where users were progressively nudged toward increasingly sensational, conspiracy-driven, or extreme political content to sustain engagement
D) A legal requirement for viewers to pass a university history exam before watching sports clips
questions.explanation: Because high-arousal and conspiratorial content holds viewer attention longer, recommendation algorithms optimizing for watch time inadvertently pushed users down extreme rabbit holes.

questions.question: Why do audio and video 'Deepfakes' pose an unprecedented threat to democratic elections and judicial evidence compared to traditional photo retouching?
options: A) They physically erase the hard drives of television newsroom computer servers
B) They prevent citizens from registering to vote in local municipal council elections
C) They can only be viewed on computer monitors located inside government military bunkers
D) They generate hyper-realistic, fabricated audiovisual recordings of public figures speaking words they never uttered, eroding public trust in visual evidence itself ('the liar's dividend')
questions.explanation: Deepfakes manufacture convincing synthetic video and voice clones, undermining the epistemological certainty of visual documentation and allowing corrupt actors to dismiss real evidence as fake ('liar's dividend').

questions.question: What is the global unique address used to locate and identify a specific webpage or file on the World Wide Web (such as https://www.example.com)?
options: A) URL (Uniform Resource Locator)
B) CPU (Central Processing Unit)
C) RAM (Random Access Memory)
D) GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)
questions.explanation: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) specifies the distinct network address where a webpage, image, or document resides on the web.

questions.question: How does 'Hypertextuality' enhance an online news article compared to a traditional printed newspaper article?
options: A) It restricts the article to exactly twelve words of plain text without any pictures
B) It allows journalists to embed clickable links directly into the text, enabling readers to explore source documents, past coverage, and primary data non-linearly
C) It converts the article into a physical paper scroll mailed through the postal service
D) It requires the reader to read the article backwards from the final sentence
questions.explanation: Hypertextuality liberates news from linear constraints, embedding hyperlinks to primary sources, archives, and contextual background.

questions.question: Subscription-based digital video services (such as Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, or Disney+ Hotstar) that allow users to stream movies and series on-demand are classified as:
options: A) AM Radio Syndicates
B) Community Newspaper Presses
C) OTT (Over-The-Top) / SVOD platforms
D) Analog Terrestrial Relay Networks
questions.explanation: OTT (Over-the-Top) platforms deliver video content directly to viewers over the internet, bypassing traditional cable, broadcast, and satellite intermediaries.

questions.question: What is the fundamental founding principle of 'Net Neutrality'?
options: A) Every internet user must pay an identical flat monthly tax of five hundred rupees to the United Nations
B) All computer monitors manufactured in the world must display the exact same screen brightness
C) Governments must ban all commercial search engines and allow only state-run web browsers
D) Internet Service Providers (ISPs) must treat all data on the internet equally, without blocking, throttling, or charging discriminatory fees for specific websites, services, or platforms
questions.explanation: Net neutrality demands that ISPs treat all internet traffic equally, prohibiting paid prioritization, throttling, or discriminatory blocking.

questions.question: In contemporary investigative data journalism, what does 'Crowdsourcing' involve?
options: A) Paying thousands of professional models to attend promotional movie premiere screenings
B) Enlisting a large community of readers or citizens to collectively review documents, report local data, or contribute eyewitness evidence to a shared investigation
C) Selling the newspaper printing press factory to a private commercial real estate developer
D) Hiring armed private security guards to block readers from entering the newsroom building
questions.explanation: Crowdsourcing harnesses the collective intelligence, time, and observations of the public to analyze large data sets, audit documents, or document widespread local phenomena.

questions.topic: New Media: Cyber Law and Governance
questions.sub_topic: Information Technology Act, 2000 (India): Section 43A and Data Privacy
questions.question: Under Section 43A of India's Information Technology Act, 2000, what legal liability is imposed on a corporate body that handles 'Sensitive Personal Data or Information' (SPDI)?
options: A) It is required to publish all personal user passwords in daily morning printed newspapers
B) It must automatically transfer fifty percent of its corporate shares to the state government
C) It is completely immune from any legal liability or financial penalty under all Indian laws
D) It is liable to pay compensation for damages to the affected person if it is negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices, leading to wrongful loss or disclosure
questions.explanation: Section 43A of the IT Act mandates that body corporates possessing sensitive personal data must implement reasonable security practices; negligence resulting in wrongful loss or disclosure requires paying damages.
